## Statement

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $\Omega$ on one side. Put $S=\partial\Omega$. Then $S$ is compact and has a finite cover by graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ that are $C^1$ homeomorphisms onto $S\cap O_j$, have derivative of rank two everywhere, and have $C^1$ coordinate transitions and a finite subordinate nonnegative smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with supports compactly contained in $O_j$ and sum one on $S$. For every continuous $f:S\to\mathbb R$, define
$$\int_S f\,dS:=\sum_j\int_{\mathbb R^2} g_j(y)\,dy,\qquad g_j(y)=\begin{cases}\chi_j(X_j(y))f(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))},&y\in U_j,\\0,&y\notin U_j.\end{cases}$$
The right-hand integrals are Riemann integrals of continuous compactly supported functions, and the finite sum is independent of the charts and partition. In graph coordinates $X(y)=(y,h(y))$ the area density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. The outward unit normal is $(-Dh,1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ for the subgraph side, transported by the rigid chart, and is continuous and independent of charts. Vector and tensor surface integrals are componentwise; flux means $\int_S F\cdot n\,dS$ for continuous $F$. All these integrals are finite. The empty surface has zero integral. If additionally the Axiom of Countable Choice is assumed, meaning that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function, then these same continuous-field surface integrals agree with the finite-chart Lebesgue surface integrals with the same Gram density.

## Statement references

[Hunter, Notes on Partial Differential Equations, §§1.9.2 and 1.10.2–1.10.3, printed pp. 12–16](https://www.math.ucdavis.edu/~hunter/pdes/pde_notes.pdf)

[Taylor, Introduction to Analysis in Several Variables, §3.2, printed pp. 119–123](https://mtaylor.web.unc.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/16915/2018/04/analmv.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The bounded open set with locally one-sided $C^1$ graph boundary and continuous scalar or vector fields on its boundary.

[F1] A closed bounded Euclidean set is compact. ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]])

[F2] The standard smooth step $\sigma$ is smooth, takes values in $[0,1]$, equals zero on $(-\infty,0]$, and equals one on $[1,\infty)$. ([[def-the-standard-smooth-step-function]])

[F3] Compactly supported Riemann integrands transform under injective $C^1$ maps with invertible derivative on their open domain by the absolute Jacobian formula. ([[cor-change-of-variables-for-compactly-supported-functions]])

[F4] The chain rule, Gram determinant and determinant multiplicativity give the surface-density transformation law. ([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]], [[thm-determinant-multiplicative]], [[thm-determinant-of-transpose]], [[thm-gram-determinant-detects-linear-independence]])

[F5] Continuous functions on compact rectangles are Riemann integrable, finite sums integrate linearly, and compact-support integrals do not depend on the containing rectangle. ([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]], [[thm-multidimensional-integral-properties]], [[lem-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-is-well-defined]])

[F6] [[lem-bounded-borel-riemann-integrands-on-boxes-have-equal-lebesgue-integrals]]: assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, a bounded Borel Riemann-integrable function on a nondegenerate box in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge1$, is Lebesgue integrable there with the same integral. Here Countable Choice means that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function ([[def-countable-choice]]); this extra premise is used only for the conditional agreement assertion.

## Proof

1.1 The boundary is closed and bounded, hence compact by F1. Consider the family of all available local one-sided graph neighborhoods and all smaller ambient chart neighborhoods whose compact closures lie inside such neighborhoods. This family covers $S$; compactness retains finitely many smaller neighborhoods and their corresponding charts, without selecting a chart separately for every point. The partition is constructed explicitly in the next two steps. Each graph chart is a homeomorphism onto its image, has rank two, and has $C^1$ transitions: on an overlap the inverse of the second graph chart is its rigid-coordinate projection onto the two base coordinates. [given, F1, F2]

2.1 Consider all rational centers $a\in\mathbb Q^3$ and positive rational radii $r<R$ for which $\overline B_R(a)$ lies inside one original chart neighborhood $O_j$. Assign each pair to the least such index $j$. Their inner balls $B_r(a)$ cover $S$, since every point has a small ball inside one chart neighborhood, and rational centers and radii can be chosen with a strict margin around that point. F1 retains finitely many inner balls covering $S$. For each retained pair put $s_l=(r_l+R_l)/2$ and $$b_l(x)=\sigma\!\left(\frac{s_l^2-|x-a_l|^2}{s_l^2-r_l^2}\right).$$ By F2 each $b_l$ is smooth, between zero and one, equals one on $\overline B_{r_l}(a_l)$ and has support in $\overline B_{s_l}(a_l)\Subset O_{j(l)}$. This is a finite explicit selection from one covering family, with no countable-choice premise. [step 1.1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.2 On an overlap write $X=Y\circ T$. The transition is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of open subsets of $\mathbb R^2$. F4 gives $DX=(DY\circ T)DT$ and hence $J_X=(J_Y\circ T)|\det DT|$, with $J_X=\sqrt{\det(DX^TDX)}$. The regularity makes both Gram densities positive. F3 transfers each continuously weighted integral whose support is compact inside that overlap between its two coordinate descriptions. [step 1.1, F3, F4]

3.1 Put $s=\sum_l b_l$ and $\theta=\sigma(4s-1)$. Then $s\ge1$ on $S$ and $\theta=1$ on the neighborhood $\{s>1/2\}$ of $S$. For $s>0$ define $c_l=\theta b_l/s$, and extend it by zero on $s=0$. Since $\theta=0$ where $s\le1/4$, this extension is smooth. Each $c_l$ is nonnegative with compact support inside $O_{j(l)}$. Put $\chi_j=\sum_{l:j(l)=j}c_l$, using zero for an empty index set. Then each support is a finite union of compact subsets of $O_j$, and $\sum_j\chi_j=\theta=1$ near $S$. [step 2.1, F2, algebra]

4.1 For each $j$, $S\cap\operatorname{supp}\chi_j$ is compact and contained in $S\cap O_j$. Its inverse under $X_j$ is compact inside $U_j$. Thus $g_j$ vanishes outside a compact subset of $U_j$, its extension by zero is continuous on $\mathbb R^2$, and F5 makes its integral finite and independent of the containing rectangle. [step 1.1, step 3.1, F5]

5.1 Given two chart partitions $\chi_j$ and $\eta_k$, insert $\sum_k\eta_k=1$ in each integral of the first sum. The support on $S$ of each $\chi_j\eta_k$ is compact inside both chart neighborhoods, so step 2.2 transfers this continuous overlap integrand to the second chart. Finite linearity in F5 and $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ recover exactly the second sum, proving chart and partition independence. [step 4.1, step 2.2, F5]

6.1 The graph derivative has columns $(e_i,\partial_i h)$, so its Gram matrix has entries $G_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+\partial_i h\,\partial_j h$ for $i,j\in\{1,2\}$, and $\det G=(1+(\partial_1h)^2)(1+(\partial_2h)^2)-(\partial_1h)^2(\partial_2h)^2=1+|Dh|^2$. The vector $(-Dh,1)$ is perpendicular to both tangent columns and points out of the subgraph. On overlaps both graph descriptions have the same tangent plane; of its two unit normals the exterior side selects the same one. For the upper-side region the outward normal is the negative of the displayed subgraph normal. Rigid coordinate maps transport the chosen exterior-side vector, including orientation-reversing maps, by their orthogonal linear part; the exterior-side criterion still gives agreement on overlaps. The graph formula is continuous. Componentwise finite linearity and the continuous dot product give all vector, tensor and flux assertions. [step 5.1, F4, F5, algebra]

7.1 For the conditional agreement assertion only, assume Countable Choice. By step 4.1 each zero-extended $g_j$ is continuous and compactly supported in $\mathbb R^2$, hence bounded and Borel on a containing nondegenerate closed rectangle and Riemann integrable there. Apply F6 with $n=2$ to this rectangle. Its Riemann and Lebesgue integrals agree, and it vanishes outside the rectangle. Equality term by term in the finite chart sum gives equality of the continuous-field surface integrals; step 5.1 already makes the Riemann sum independent of the chosen charts and partition. This imports no Countable Choice premise into the preceding construction or independence proof, and asserts no extension to arbitrary measurable surface fields. [given, F6, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

before.statement:
Use the nonrelativistic Newtonian spacetime $I\times E$, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an open interval with absolute time $t$ in seconds. Here $E$ is a three-dimensional oriented Euclidean affine space: its translation vectors form an oriented Euclidean vector space, but no origin in $E$ is distinguished. A **Cartesian inertial chart** supplies an orientation-preserving affine isometry $x:E\to\mathbb R^3$ and the absolute-time coordinate. Write $\mathrm{SO}(3)=\{Q\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:Q^TQ=I_3,\det Q=1\}$. Inertial charts are related by

$$t^*=t+t_0,\qquad x^*=Qx+vt+a,$$

where $t_0$ is a constant time translation in seconds, $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is constant, $v\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant relative velocity in m s$^{-1}$, and $a\in\mathbb R^3$ is a constant spatial translation in metres. A **worldline** is a curve $t\mapsto(t,x(t))$ with $x\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$, parameterized by absolute time; this model imposes no relativistic speed or causal condition. A **rigid observer change** is the more general coordinate change $t^*=t,\ x^*=Q(t)x+c(t)$, with $Q\in C^2(I,\mathrm{SO}(3))$ and $c\in C^2(I,\mathbb R^3)$ in metres; it is not called inertial unless $Q$ is constant and $c$ is affine in time. A frame here means an adapted Cartesian chart, not an observer congruence or a basis field.

For the initial-chart material-motion convention below, require $0\in I$. $$\int_S f\,dS:=\sum_j\int_{\mathbb R^2} g_j(y)\,dy,\qquad g_j(y)=\begin{cases}\chi_j(X_j(y))f(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))},&y\in U_j,\\0,&y\notin U_j.\end{cases}$$

after.statement:
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded open set whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $\Omega$ on one side. Put $S=\partial\Omega$. Then $S$ is compact and has a finite cover by graph charts $X_j:U_j\subset\mathbb R^2\to S\cap O_j$ that are $C^1$ homeomorphisms onto $S\cap O_j$, have derivative of rank two everywhere, and have $C^1$ coordinate transitions and a finite subordinate nonnegative smooth ambient partition $\chi_j$ with supports compactly contained in $O_j$ and sum one on $S$. For every continuous $f:S\to\mathbb R$, define
$$\int_S f\,dS:=\sum_j\int_{\mathbb R^2} g_j(y)\,dy,\qquad g_j(y)=\begin{cases}\chi_j(X_j(y))f(X_j(y))\sqrt{\det(DX_j(y)^TDX_j(y))},&y\in U_j,\\0,&y\notin U_j.\end{cases}$$
The right-hand integrals are Riemann integrals of continuous compactly supported functions, and the finite sum is independent of the charts and partition. In graph coordinates $X(y)=(y,h(y))$ the area density is $\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$. The outward unit normal is $(-Dh,1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$ for the subgraph side, transported by the rigid chart, and is continuous and independent of charts. Vector and tensor surface integrals are componentwise; flux means $\int_S F\cdot n\,dS$ for continuous $F$. All these integrals are finite. The empty surface has zero integral. If additionally the Axiom of Countable Choice is assumed, meaning that every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function, then these same continuous-field surface integrals agree with the finite-chart Lebesgue surface integrals with the same Gram density.

after.statement:
Adopt a smooth single-component material continuum on a stated macroscopic regime in a Cartesian inertial chart. Let $\rho_0\in C^1(\overline B)$ be positive. On each swept material region, require $\rho,u,e,T,s,q,\sigma\in C^1$ and $b,r\in C^0$, with $\rho>0$ and $T>0$; the motion has the regularity and positive Jacobian in the preceding definition. A material subregion is $\chi_t(V)$ for a nonempty bounded open set $V\Subset B$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid coordinate change, a $C^1$ graph with $V$ on one side; its boundary moves with the material velocity. The Jordan integral convention for such regions and their smooth images is the one in the mathematical interface identified below. The continuum approximation, its empirical regime, and the following balance laws are physical assumptions of this model, not deductions from the mathematical definition of a motion or from molecular mechanics.

Assume there are no mass sources and no diffusion relative to $u$. Adopt a positive reference mass density $\rho_0$, a positive current density $\rho$, a body-acceleration field $b$, a contact traction $t(t,x,n)=\sigma(t,x)n$ depending only on the local outward unit normal $n$, a $C^1$ Cauchy stress field $\sigma$, specific internal energy $e$, positive temperature $T$, specific entropy $s$, heat-flux vector $q$, and specific heat supply $r$, with the types and SI units fixed in the preceding definition. Contact traction and volume-force densities are continuous and locally bounded on the smooth material regions under consideration. There are no surface couples or intrinsic spin angular momentum; a micropolar or couple-stress model is outside this postulate.

For every such material subregion, adopt conservation of mass,

$$\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(t,x)\,dx=\int_V\rho_0(a)\,da.$$

In the same inertial chart, adopt the balances of linear and angular momentum,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\,dS,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho u)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}x\times(\rho b)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}x\times t(t,x,n)\,dS.$$

Adopt the total-energy balance and entropy inequality

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho\left(e+\frac{|u|^2}{2}\right)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho b\cdot u\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}t(t,x,n)\cdot u\,dS-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}q\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho r\,dx,$$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho s\,dx\ge-\int_{\partial\chi_t(V)}\frac{q}{T}\cdot n\,dS+\int_{\chi_t(V)}\frac{\rho r}{T}\,dx.$$

The entropy flux uses the local material temperature at the heat-transfer point. A reservoir at a different temperature, a singular surface force, a shock, vacuum, or a weak solution requires a separately stated model and is not covered here. The postulate reports no experiment and asserts no measurement or universal claim that nature obeys these assumptions.

after.statement: Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open time interval containing $0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^1$ reference domain, and let $\chi\in C^2(I\times U,\mathbb R^3)$ be an orientation-preserving family of diffeomorphisms on an open neighborhood $U\supseteq\overline B$, with $\chi(0,a)=a$ and $J(t,a)=\det D_a\chi(t,a)>0$. Set $u(t,\chi(t,a))=\partial_t\chi(t,a)$. Let the current density $\rho\in C^1$ be positive on the swept material region, and define $\rho_0(a)=\rho(0,a)$. Assume the adopted single-component mass balance with no sources or diffusion relative to $u$, on every bounded $C^1$ material subregion. Then this integral material-mass balance is equivalent, under these smoothness hypotheses, to $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$. It also forces $\rho(t,\chi(t,a))J(t,a)=\rho_0(a)$. Consequently, for positive density, $D_t\rho=0$ throughout the material region if and only if $\operatorname{div}u=0$ there. This is a conditional deduction within the adopted smooth model; it asserts no result for vacuum, shocks, weak solutions, or empirical applicability.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $\beta$ be the standard flat function. The **standard smooth step function** is
$$ \sigma(t):=\frac{\beta(t)}{\beta(t)+\beta(1-t)}. $$
Because $\beta$ is smooth and positive on $(0,\infty)$, the denominator is positive on $(0,1)$, while $\sigma(t)=0$ for $t\le 0$ and $\sigma(t)=1$ for $t\ge 1$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, with $Dg(x)$ invertible on $U$. Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be compactly supported Riemann integrable and suppose $\operatorname{supp}f\subseteq g(U)$. Define
$$h(x)=\begin{cases}f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|,&x\in U,\\0,&x\notin U.\end{cases}$$
Then $h$ is compactly supported Riemann integrable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(y)\,dy=\int_{\mathbb R^n}h(x)\,dx.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For a finite list $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ in a real or complex inner product space ([[def-inner-product-space]]), its **Gram matrix** is

$$G(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1}):=(\langle v_i,v_j\rangle)_{i,j<r}\in M_r(\mathbb F),$$

using the square matrix space [[def-matrix-space]]. Its **Gram determinant** is the determinant ([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]) $\det G(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$. For the empty list, the Gram matrix is the unique $0\times0$ matrix and its determinant is $1$.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

For every $n\ge1$, every commutative ring $R$, and every $A\in M_n(R)$,
$$\det(A^{\mathsf T})=\det(A).$$

For every finite list $(v_0,\ldots,v_{r-1})$ in a real or complex inner product space, its Gram determinant is a nonnegative real number. It is positive if and only if the list is linearly independent, and it is zero if and only if the list is linearly dependent. The empty Gram determinant is $1$.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ have compact support. If $f$ is Riemann integrable on one closed rectangle whose interior contains its support, then it is integrable on every such rectangle, and all the resulting integrals are equal. This includes the empty-support case.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $n\ge1$, let $Q=\prod_{j=1}^n[a_j,b_j]$ with $a_j<b_j$, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and Borel. If $f$ is Riemann integrable, then $f\in L^1(\lambda_n|_Q)$ and its Lebesgue and Riemann integrals agree.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The boundary is closed and bounded, hence compact by F1. Consider the family of all available local one-sided graph neighborhoods and all smaller ambient chart neighborhoods whose compact closures lie inside such neighborhoods. This family covers $S$; compactness retains finitely many smaller neighborhoods and their corresponding charts, without selecting a chart separately for every point. The partition is constructed explicitly in the next two steps. Each graph chart is a homeomorphism onto its image, has rank two, and has $C^1$ transitions: on an overlap the inverse of the second graph chart is its rigid-coordinate projection onto the two base coordinates.

Consider all rational centers $a\in\mathbb Q^3$ and positive rational radii $r<R$ for which $\overline B_R(a)$ lies inside one original chart neighborhood $O_j$. Assign each pair to the least such index $j$. Their inner balls $B_r(a)$ cover $S$, since every point has a small ball inside one chart neighborhood, and rational centers and radii can be chosen with a strict margin around that point. F1 retains finitely many inner balls covering $S$. For each retained pair put $s_l=(r_l+R_l)/2$ and $$b_l(x)=\sigma\!\left(\frac{s_l^2-|x-a_l|^2}{s_l^2-r_l^2}\right).$$ By F2 each $b_l$ is smooth, between zero and one, equals one on $\overline B_{r_l}(a_l)$ and has support in $\overline B_{s_l}(a_l)\Subset O_{j(l)}$. This is a finite explicit selection from one covering family, with no countable-choice premise.

On an overlap write $X=Y\circ T$. The transition is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism of open subsets of $\mathbb R^2$. F4 gives $DX=(DY\circ T)DT$ and hence $J_X=(J_Y\circ T)|\det DT|$, with $J_X=\sqrt{\det(DX^TDX)}$. The regularity makes both Gram densities positive. F3 transfers each continuously weighted integral whose support is compact inside that overlap between its two coordinate descriptions.

Put $s=\sum_l b_l$ and $\theta=\sigma(4s-1)$. Then $s\ge1$ on $S$ and $\theta=1$ on the neighborhood $\{s>1/2\}$ of $S$. For $s>0$ define $c_l=\theta b_l/s$, and extend it by zero on $s=0$. Since $\theta=0$ where $s\le1/4$, this extension is smooth. Each $c_l$ is nonnegative with compact support inside $O_{j(l)}$. Put $\chi_j=\sum_{l:j(l)=j}c_l$, using zero for an empty index set. Then each support is a finite union of compact subsets of $O_j$, and $\sum_j\chi_j=\theta=1$ near $S$.

For each $j$, $S\cap\operatorname{supp}\chi_j$ is compact and contained in $S\cap O_j$. Its inverse under $X_j$ is compact inside $U_j$. Thus $g_j$ vanishes outside a compact subset of $U_j$, its extension by zero is continuous on $\mathbb R^2$, and F5 makes its integral finite and independent of the containing rectangle.

Given two chart partitions $\chi_j$ and $\eta_k$, insert $\sum_k\eta_k=1$ in each integral of the first sum. The support on $S$ of each $\chi_j\eta_k$ is compact inside both chart neighborhoods, so step 2.2 transfers this continuous overlap integrand to the second chart. Finite linearity in F5 and $\sum_j\chi_j=1$ recover exactly the second sum, proving chart and partition independence.

The graph derivative has columns $(e_i,\partial_i h)$, so its Gram matrix has entries $G_{ij}=\delta_{ij}+\partial_i h\,\partial_j h$ for $i,j\in\{1,2\}$, and $\det G=(1+(\partial_1h)^2)(1+(\partial_2h)^2)-(\partial_1h)^2(\partial_2h)^2=1+|Dh|^2$. The vector $(-Dh,1)$ is perpendicular to both tangent columns and points out of the subgraph. On overlaps both graph descriptions have the same tangent plane; of its two unit normals the exterior side selects the same one. For the upper-side region the outward normal is the negative of the displayed subgraph normal. Rigid coordinate maps transport the chosen exterior-side vector, including orientation-reversing maps, by their orthogonal linear part; the exterior-side criterion still gives agreement on overlaps. The graph formula is continuous. Componentwise finite linearity and the continuous dot product give all vector, tensor and flux assertions.

For the conditional agreement assertion only, assume Countable Choice. By step 4.1 each zero-extended $g_j$ is continuous and compactly supported in $\mathbb R^2$, hence bounded and Borel on a containing nondegenerate closed rectangle and Riemann integrable there. Apply F6 with $n=2$ to this rectangle. Its Riemann and Lebesgue integrals agree, and it vanishes outside the rectangle. Equality term by term in the finite chart sum gives equality of the continuous-field surface integrals; step 5.1 already makes the Riemann sum independent of the chosen charts and partition. This imports no Countable Choice premise into the preceding construction or independence proof, and asserts no extension to arbitrary measurable surface fields.

The explicit auxiliary empty-surface convention is zero (Statement final sentence); no chart or normal is requested on an empty surface. A zero-sum chart partition also gives zero. Source: Statement nonempty Omega and empty-surface sentence.

Continuous f=0 makes every g_j=0, so its finite Riemann sum is zero; componentwise zero fields and zero flux obey the same formula. No division by f or flux appears. Source: Statement displayed definition, step4.1 and5.1.

A single global chart/one partition term, whenever available, gives exactly its weighted patch integral. The theorem does not require a compact closed nonempty boundary to admit one global open graph chart. One local graph has rank2 and density sqrt(1+|Dh|²)>0 even for flat h. Rank-two chart derivatives make Gram determinant positive, so no singular chart is admitted. Flat graph Dh=0 gives density1 and normals ±e3. Disconnected domains, holes and multiple boundary components remain allowed; all are covered by the finite compact-boundary argument and exterior-side choice. No connectedness or lower bound for curvature is assumed. Source: Statement local graph/rank hypothesis; steps1.1,2.2,6.1.
